docs.title: nomospice
docs.text: nomospice is a circuit simulator with schematic capture and click-to-probe waveforms. You draw a circuit, run it with ngspice, and click a wire or a part to plot its voltage or current. It reads and writes the widespread .asc schematic format, writes SPICE for you through forms that show what they write, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Where to go
docs.text:
• Tutorials: learn nomospice by doing. Four short lessons, from a first simulation to your own blocks.
  • How-to guides: recipes for particular tasks, such as using a model library, measuring with cursors, poles and zeros, or several windows.
  • Reference: every key and menu item, the analyses and directives, the plot window, files, and the command line.
  • Explanation: how a simulation runs, how blocks become subcircuits, and how nomospice relates to other simulators.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text: Install the signed macOS app or the Windows installer from the releases. Both include ngspice and update themselves. nomospice is free software under the AGPL-3.0-or-later.

docs.title: How this documentation is made
docs.text: This documentation follows the Diátaxis framework: tutorials teach by doing, how-to guides solve particular tasks, the reference lists facts, and the explanation gives background. Its sources are the Markdown files in docs/ of the repository; MkDocs with the Material theme makes the website.

docs.title: Build the website
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve            # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000, rebuilt on every change
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict   # the site in site/
python3 scripts/check-docs.py site

check-docs.py checks that every picture and link resolves, that every picture is used, and that the built site fetches nothing from third parties (no web fonts, no scripts from elsewhere). CI runs the same.

docs.title: Publish the website
docs.text:
The site is served by GitHub Pages from the branch gh-pages, which only ever holds the built site:

.venv/bin/mkdocs gh-deploy --strict    # builds, commits the site to gh-pages and pushes it

It is at https://mprotogerakis.github.io/nomospice/ a minute later.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Every picture comes from the real app, played by a scene: docs/scenes/<name>.js drives a development build of nomospice as a user would, pressing keys, clicking the schematic and filling in dialogs, and every shot(id) saves a picture of the window as docs/img/<name>/<id>.png.

scripts/docs-shots.sh                    # every scene (macOS)
scripts/docs-shots.sh first-circuit      # one

A scene is a function of app:

export default async function (app) {
  await app.theme("light");
  await app.key("r");                    // a key, as pressed on the schematic
  await app.click([192, 48]);            // a click at a schematic point
  await app.doubleClick([224, 128]);     // edit the part there
  await app.fill("Value", "100n");       // a field of the open dialog, by its label
  await app.ok();
  await app.key("Enter", { metaKey: true });
  await app.shot("01-run");              // docs/img/<scene>/01-run.png
}

Other helpers: move, rightClick, type (into a field by selector), press (a button, tab or menu item by its text), clickAt and menuAt (an element by selector), load (a schematic as items, saved in the scene's own folder), example (one of the app's examples), command (a menu bar command by its id), setPlot (cursors, zoom), useS (the app's state) and invoke (a backend command). See src/scenes.ts.

With pngquant installed, the pictures are stored with a palette of their own, a quarter of the size. The app runs under its own identifier, so the installed app's settings and recovery files are not touched, and git commits a scene makes are signed by nomospice docs. Change the app, run the scenes again, and the pictures are current.

docs.title: Videos (experimental)
docs.text:
Every tutorial can be turned into a narrated video. The system voices do not sound good enough yet, so the videos are not published:

nix shell nixpkgs#ffmpeg -c scripts/docs-video.py docs/tutorial/*.md    # into build/videos/

Each picture of the page is shown while the text that follows it is spoken; the page's title and the text before the first picture are spoken over the first one. Code, tables and notes are not spoken, so a page can say more than its video; a heading is spoken only where its section has text before the next picture, such as the closing summary. The spoken text is in the video as subtitles and beside it as an .srt file. The speech comes from macOS say (NOMOSPICE_VOICE picks a voice) or from espeak-ng.

So write a tutorial as pictures, each followed by a short paragraph that says what to do and what you see.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: Download nomospice_x.y.z_aarch64.dmg from the releases, open it and drag nomospice into Applications. The app is signed and notarized, needs a Mac with Apple Silicon and macOS 11 or later, and includes ngspice.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: Download nomospice_x.y.z_x64-setup.exe (or the .msi) from the releases and run it. It includes ngspice. The installer is not code-signed yet: if SmartScreen warns, choose More info → Run anyway.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: From version 0.1.5 on, nomospice looks for a newer release when it starts. If there is one, the status bar shows Update x.y.z; click it to install. Check for Updates… in the app menu (macOS) or the Help menu (Windows) looks right away. Updates are signed and checked against a key built into the app.

docs.title: Linux and building from source
docs.text:
There are no Linux packages yet; nomospice builds from source on Linux, macOS and Windows. You need Rust, Node 20 or later, pnpm, and the ngspice shared library (apt install libngspice0, brew install libngspice):

git clone https://github.com/mprotogerakis/nomospice
cd nomospice
pnpm install
pnpm tauri dev

pnpm tauri build makes installers. nomospice looks for ngspice in NGSPICE_LIB, next to its executable, in the usual Homebrew and Linux paths, and through the system loader.

docs.title: Model libraries (optional)
docs.text: nomospice comes with its own symbols and a few default models (1N4148, 2N3904, 2N3906, switches). For more, add a model library: see Use model libraries.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Background: why nomospice works the way it does.

  • How a simulation runs: from the drawing to the netlist, to ngspice, to the plot.
  • Hierarchy: how a block becomes a subcircuit, and where its parameters come from.
  • One ngspice, many windows: what is shared between windows, and what is not.
  • Compatibility: files from other simulators, model libraries, and what nomospice ships.

docs.title: Schematics
docs.text: nomospice reads and writes the .asc schematic format that is widespread in teaching and in vendors' application notes. Opening and saving a file keeps it as it was, including lines nomospice does not understand; it is written in Latin-1, or in UTF-16 where its characters need it. A schematic you draw in nomospice opens elsewhere, as long as it uses parts and directives that simulator knows.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
The schematics are simulated with ngspice, an open-source SPICE. Most dot commands mean the same in every SPICE. Where schematics in the .asc world use forms of their own, nomospice handles them when it writes the netlist and runs it:

  • .step, including nested sweeps and Monte Carlo runs with mc(), flat() and gauss(), each step a run of its own;
  • .meas in its common syntax, measured per step;
  • Laplace= sources;
  • blocks and the parameters passed to them.

Some features of other simulators have no counterpart in ngspice. The log tells you what ngspice did not accept.

docs.title: Model libraries
docs.text:
Vendors publish SPICE models for their parts. Many of them work in ngspice as they are, some need features ngspice lacks. nomospice can use:

  • your own folders of model files;
  • the freeware Micro-Cap 12 library, downloaded from the Internet Archive on request: about 45,000 models and subcircuits;
  • the libraries of an installed LTspice, which it finds by itself.

docs.title: What nomospice ships
docs.text:
nomospice is free software under the AGPL-3.0-or-later and contains code from OpenPCB. It ships ngspice and its own symbols and default models, and none of the files of other simulators or of the Micro-Cap package: they are used where they are installed or downloaded by you. The licenses of everything included are listed under About (ⓘ in the toolbar).

LTspice is a trademark of Analog Devices, Inc.; Micro-Cap is a trademark of Spectrum Software. nomospice is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

docs.title: Hierarchy
docs.text: A block is a part that stands for a schematic. It lets you draw a circuit once and use it many times, and keeps large circuits readable.

docs.title: What makes a block
docs.text: A symbol is a block when a schematic of the same name lies beside it, and the symbol calls for one: its type is block, or it is a subcircuit call (prefix X) without a model of its own. Create block symbol makes such a symbol from a schematic. The pins are the schematic's labels marked as ports, matched by name: inputs on the left, outputs on the right.

docs.title: What runs
docs.text:
When a schematic uses a block, nomospice netlists the block's schematic as a subcircuit, .subckt, with the ports as its connections, and places it with an X line. A block inside a block works the same way. Nets inside a block are its own: a label mid inside does not connect to a mid outside, except through a port. The ground 0 is everywhere the same ground.

A block's schematic keeps what it needs as a subcircuit: its parts, its .param, .model and .include directives, and its .ic. Its analyses and .meas directives are its own business when you open it on its own, and are left out of the subcircuit.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A block can take parameters, as a part takes its value:

  1. the block's own value, R=10k, wins;
  2. else a .param R=1k in the block's schematic is the default;
  3. else the value of R in the schematic above is used.

So a block can be configured where it is placed, have a sensible default, or simply follow the circuit around it.

docs.title: What is refused
docs.text: Some things cannot be a subcircuit, and nomospice says so in the warnings instead of netlisting something wrong: a block that places itself (directly or through others), a schematic that lacks a label for one of the symbol's pins, a port on ground, two ports on the same net, or a schematic that cannot be read.

docs.title: How a simulation runs
docs.text: A schematic is a drawing; ngspice understands a netlist. Between the two, nomospice does what a careful person would do by hand, every time you run.

docs.title: From the drawing to nets
docs.text:
Wires that touch at their ends or at a pin form a net. A wire crossing another without a dot is not connected. A net label gives its net a name; two labels of the same name connect their nets, even far apart, so labels save wires. The label 0 is the ground, the reference every voltage is measured against. A circuit without a ground cannot be solved, and nomospice warns about it.

Nets without a label get numbered names, N001, N002 …, which may change when you edit. Labels are names you can rely on, in the plot and in .meas directives.

docs.title: From nets to a netlist
docs.text:
Every part becomes one line: its instance name, the nets at its pins in the order its symbol defines, its value, and its model. Directives are copied as written. Model definitions from libraries, and the definitions they depend on, are added; a block becomes a subcircuit (see Hierarchy). Cmd+L shows the netlist.

What runs is slightly more than that. nomospice adds 0 V sources as current sensors, so that every part's current can be plotted, in AC analyses with its phase too. It copies included files into the netlist, so ngspice never opens a file itself, and it removes .control blocks, which ngspice would execute on loading, shell commands included. as simulated in the netlist panel shows this version, and the log's line numbers refer to it.

docs.title: The run
docs.text: ngspice runs inside nomospice, as a library. It reads the netlist, solves the circuit for the analysis, and keeps the results as vectors: one per node voltage and current, over time, frequency or the swept value. Halt asks it to stop; what it computed so far is kept.

docs.title: From the results to the plot
docs.text:
Nothing is copied until you ask for it: clicking a wire or a part asks ngspice for that one vector, evaluated as an expression, and the plot draws it. That is why plotting is instant even for long runs, and why an expression like V(in)*I(R1) costs nothing extra: ngspice evaluates it.

Each run has a number. The results nomospice shows belong to one run, and when you change the schematic they are marked stale until you run again. Live mode simply runs again shortly after each edit.

docs.title: Result tabs
docs.text: A schematic can hold several analyses: the one SPICE runs, and alternatives kept as comments. Each gets a result tab with its own traces, zoom and cursors. Switching tabs runs that analysis in place of the other, so the schematic stays a valid file that other programs read as before, with one active analysis.

docs.title: One ngspice, many windows
docs.text: Each window of nomospice is its own document: its schematic, its undo history, its results, zoom and cursors. Some things are shared by all windows of the app.

docs.title: Shared: the engine
docs.text:
ngspice runs inside nomospice as a library, once. It can run one simulation at a time and holds the results of the latest run only. So:

  • When two windows run at the same moment, the second waits for the first.
  • When window B runs after window A, A's results are no longer in ngspice. A's plot is unaffected: what is drawn has been copied out. But adding a trace or exporting in A needs the results again, and nomospice runs A's analysis once more first.
  • Halt stops only the run of its own window, and closing a window stops its run.

docs.title: Shared: libraries and symbols
docs.text: The model libraries are the app's, not a window's. When you change them in one window, every window loads its parts anew. A symbol saved in one window is drawn anew in every window with a schematic in that folder.

docs.title: Not shared: files
docs.text: A file is open in one window at most. Opening it again brings that window to the front, and Save As refuses a file another window has open, so two windows never write over each other.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: Each window keeps its own copy of its unsaved changes. After a crash every copy is offered, each in a window of its own. Quit asks the windows one after another, and a Cancel in any of them keeps them all open: a quit never half-happens.

docs.title: How-to guides
docs.text:
Recipes for particular tasks. They assume you know the basics from the tutorials.

Schematics and files

  • Open schematics, symbols and netlists
  • Use model libraries
  • Draw and edit symbols
  • Work with several windows
  • Keep a version history
  • Recover unsaved work

Simulating

  • Choose an analysis
  • Plot and measure
  • Find poles and zeros
  • Use a transfer function as a source
  • Export schematics, plots and results

Beyond the app

  • Let an AI assistant use nomospice

docs.title: Let an AI assistant use nomospice
docs.text: nomospice includes an MCP server: started with --mcp, it lets an AI assistant that speaks the Model Context Protocol read and write schematics, simulate them and search the model libraries. It uses the same libraries as the app.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
Add nomospice to the assistant's MCP configuration, with the path to the nomospice program:

{ "mcpServers": { "nomospice": { "command": "/Applications/nomospice.app/Contents/MacOS/nomospice", "args": ["--mcp"] } } }

On Windows the program is nomospice.exe in the installation folder.

docs.title: What the assistant can do
docs.text:
Tool Does simulate runs a schematic or netlist and returns the analysis, vector names, results, .meas values, warnings, the log, and the traces asked for (downsampled) netlist the SPICE netlist of a schematic, with each item's nets and each part's current expression read_schematic parts, net labels and directives of a schematic write_schematic writes .asc text to a file (an existing file only when asked to overwrite it) library_search searches the models and subcircuits of the libraries library_get the .model or .subckt text of a part, with what it depends on examples the example schematics, a good starting point for the .asc format

Open a schematic the assistant wrote in nomospice to see it, and save it from there.

docs.title: Set the analysis
docs.text:
Click the sliders in the toolbar (Simulate → Edit Simulation Command…). The form has a tab for each analysis and shows the SPICE line it writes. Click OK; a new analysis is placed where you click.

Tab Directive What you get Transient .tran voltages and currents over time AC .ac magnitude and phase over frequency (Bode, Nyquist, Nichols plots); a single frequency gives a table of phasors DC sweep .dc values over a swept source; a nested sweep gives a family of curves Noise .noise noise spectra (add the trace onoise_spectrum or inoise_spectrum) and their totals under Results DC op pnt .op a table of node voltages and currents Transfer fn .tf gain, input and output resistance at the operating point Poles/zeros .pz a map of poles and zeros: see Find poles and zeros Sensitivity .sens how much the output depends on each part (add a part's name as a trace)

You can also type the directive yourself: press S and write it in the Text tab.

docs.title: Keep several analyses
docs.text: Click the plus beside the result tabs to add another analysis. It is written as a comment under the first, so the schematic's own analysis stays as it is, and gets a result tab of its own that opens and runs at once. Each tab keeps its own traces, zoom and cursors. The cross on a tab removes its analysis from the schematic (Cmd+Z brings it back). Double-click a tab to edit its analysis.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
• Cmd+Enter (Simulate → Run) runs the analysis of the shown tab.
  • Halt (the toolbar's square while it runs) stops it; the results so far are kept, marked aborted.
  • Live mode, the lightning in the toolbar, runs again shortly after every edit.

The status bar shows the analysis that ran, and stale when the schematic changed since. Cmd+L opens the log and the netlist.

docs.title: The examples
docs.text: The start screen has an example for most analyses: rc_transient, rc_bode, diode_sweep and bjt_curves (DC sweeps), noise_rc, phasor_rlc (a single-frequency AC analysis), pz_sallen_key, and analysis_tabs with several analyses in tabs.

docs.title: The schematic as SVG
docs.text: Right-click the canvas and choose Export schematic as SVG… (or File → Export Schematic as SVG…). The SVG is drawn in a light print style, whatever theme you use, and opens in Inkscape, browsers, PowerPoint and Keynote.

docs.title: The plot as SVG
docs.text: Right-click the plot and choose Export plot as SVG… (File → Export Plot as SVG…). It has the same axes, zoom and cursors as on screen, and a legend.

docs.title: The data as CSV
docs.text: Right-click the plot and choose Copy data as CSV: the x values and one column per trace go to the clipboard, ready to paste into a spreadsheet.

docs.title: All results as a .raw file
docs.text: Right-click the plot and choose Export results as .raw… (File → Export Results as .raw…): every vector of the run in ngspice's binary raw format, for other waveform viewers and scripts. Part currents keep their names, each step of a .step becomes a plot of its own, and a noise analysis adds its totals.

docs.title: The netlist
docs.text: Cmd+L shows the netlist in the bottom panel. as simulated shows the netlist that actually ran, with current sensors and included files; the log's line numbers refer to that one. Select and copy it from there.

docs.title: Use a transfer function as a source
docs.text:
A controlled source can follow a transfer function H(s): a quick way to model a filter, a sensor or a controller without building it from parts.

  1. Place a voltage-controlled voltage source, e (or a voltage-controlled current source, g), from the component library (P).
  2. Wire its control input to the signal and its output to the load.
  3. Give it the value Laplace=1/(1+s*tau), and define the parameter with a directive: .param tau=1m.

Any ratio of polynomials in s works, and .param names may appear in it. The source works in operating point, AC and transient analyses.

The example laplace_lowpass is a first-order low-pass with τ = 1 ms: its AC tab shows the corner at 159 Hz, its Transient tab the step response 1 − e^(−t/τ).

docs.title: Use model libraries
docs.text: nomospice has its own symbols and a few default models: the diode 1N4148, the transistors 2N3904 and 2N3906, and switches. For other parts, add a model library: a folder of .lib, .sub and similar files with .model and .subckt definitions.

docs.title: Add a library
docs.text:
Press Cmd+, (nomospice → Model Libraries… on macOS, File → Model Libraries… on Windows), or click Libraries… in the component library.

  • Add folder… adds a folder of your own. Its models and subcircuits become searchable and are pulled into the netlist when a part uses them.
  • Get Micro-Cap 12 library downloads the freeware Micro-Cap 12 package from the Internet Archive (about 60 MB) and unpacks its library, about 45,000 models and subcircuits, for local use.

When two libraries define the same name, the one listed first wins. Untick a library to switch it off without removing it.

docs.title: Find and place a part
docs.text:
Press P (or F2, Cmd+K) for the component library and type a name. The tabs narrow the list to symbols, diodes, BJTs, MOSFETs, JFETs or subcircuits; the right side shows a part's description and pins. Click Place and put the part down like any other.

A subcircuit without a symbol of its own gets a generated box symbol with its pins. Its definition, and the definitions it depends on, go into the netlist by themselves.

docs.title: Give a part another model
docs.text: Right-click a diode, transistor or MOSFET and choose Choose model from library…. The component library opens on that kind of part; the one you pick replaces the part's model.

docs.title: Open a schematic
docs.text:
Press Cmd+O (File → Open…) and choose an .asc file, or drop it on the window. If the window holds nothing yet, the schematic opens there; otherwise it opens in a window of its own. A file that is open already is not opened twice: its window comes to the front.

nomospice reads .asc files in Latin-1 and UTF-16 and keeps every line it does not understand, so a schematic made elsewhere keeps its parts when you save it again. Its symbols are looked up among the built-in symbols first, then in the schematic's folder, and then in your model libraries.

docs.title: Open a symbol
docs.text: Open an .asy file the same way to edit it: see Draw and edit symbols.

docs.title: Open a netlist
docs.text: Open a .cir, .net, .sp, .spi or .ckt file and nomospice makes it a schematic of one SPICE directive that holds the whole netlist. It runs as it is, and you plot its nodes by name with Add trace. Analyses inside a .control block are turned into dot commands. The first Cmd+S asks where to save the schematic as an .asc file, so the netlist itself is never overwritten.

docs.title: Add a model file
docs.text: Drop a .lib, .sub, .mod or .inc file on a schematic: nomospice adds an .include directive for it, relative to the schematic's folder when the file is inside it.

docs.title: Plot by clicking
docs.text:
After a run, the schematic is a probe:

  • click a wire to plot its voltage;
  • click a part to plot its current, in transient, DC and AC analyses alike;
  • click near a pin of a transistor or an IC to plot that pin's current, such as Ib(Q1) or Ix(U1:OUT);
  • right-click a two-pin part and choose Plot power for the power it takes (transient and DC analyses).

Each unit gets a pane of its own: volts, amperes, watts.

docs.title: Plot an expression
docs.text: Click Add trace beside the plot and type an expression in ngspice's syntax: V(in)-V(out), I(R1), V(in)*I(R1) (in watts), db(V(out)), group_delay(V(out)). The unit follows from the expression. A constant, such as 0.5, draws a reference line.

docs.title: Arrange traces
docs.text: Right-click a trace's row in the table beside the plot to put it on a right axis with a scale of its own, to move it into another unit's pane, to plot the group delay of an AC result, to copy its expression, or to remove it.

docs.title: Measure with cursors
docs.text:
• Click to set cursor A, shift-click to set cursor B. The table shows each trace at both cursors, their difference Δ, and 1/Δx.
  • Shift-drag marks a range A–B; the table shows each trace's average, RMS and integral over it.
  • Drag to zoom, use the wheel or a trackpad to zoom and pan, double-click to see everything again.

For measurements you want every run, write a .meas directive (press S, then the Measurement tab): its result is listed beside the plot.

docs.title: Look at the spectrum
docs.text: Right-click a transient plot and choose FFT (spectrum): the spectrum of the range between the cursors A and B, else of what is shown, with a Hann window and in decibels of the amplitude. Back to the transient returns.

docs.title: Other choices in the plot's menu
docs.text: Right-click the plot for the y axis (logarithmic, or a fixed range), copying the data as CSV, exporting the plot as SVG or all results as a .raw file, and for AC results the Nyquist and Nichols plots.

docs.title: Find poles and zeros
docs.text: A .pz analysis finds the poles and zeros of a transfer function between two pairs of nodes.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Open the simulation command (the sliders in the toolbar), choose Poles/zeros, and give the input and output nodes. Or write the directive yourself, for example .pz in 0 out 0 vol pz: voltage in, voltage out, poles and zeros. The example pz_sallen_key is a second-order Sallen-Key low-pass.

The result is a map of the s-plane: × marks a pole, ○ a zero, and the right half, where a pole means the circuit is unstable, is shaded. Hover a pole for its frequency f₀ and damping ζ. The table on the right lists them all, and Results in the bottom panel lists the raw values.

docs.title: Draw a root locus
docs.text:
The root locus shows how the poles move while one value changes. In the panel on the right, give

  • Parameter: a .param name or a resistor, capacitor or inductor (such as R1),
  • From, To and the number of Steps, spaced logarithmically or linearly,

and click Draw root locus. nomospice runs one .pz analysis per step and draws each pole's path, from a dot at the start to a square at the end. Halt stops it; Clear removes it.

Drag to pan the map, use the wheel to zoom, double-click to fit it again.

docs.title: Recover unsaved work
docs.text: nomospice keeps a copy of every window's unsaved changes, written shortly after each change. A normal close or quit asks you about unsaved changes and removes the copy. If nomospice ends any other way (a crash, a forced quit, the computer turned off), the copy stays.

docs.title: Restore after a crash
docs.text:
Start nomospice again. It asks:

Restore unsaved changes to file from the last session?

  • Yes opens the schematic with your changes, marked unsaved. Save it to keep them.
  • No deletes the copy.

If several windows had unsaved changes, each is offered in a window of its own. A schematic that had never been saved asks where to save it, as it would have.

docs.title: Where the copies are
docs.text: In nomospice's data folder: ~/Library/Application Support/de.nomospice.app on macOS, %APPDATA%\de.nomospice.app on Windows, ~/.local/share/de.nomospice.app on Linux. They are named recovery-…json. You do not need to touch them.

docs.title: Draw and edit symbols
docs.text: A symbol (.asy) is how a part looks in a schematic and where its pins are. nomospice edits symbols on the same canvas as schematics.

docs.title: Open a symbol
docs.text:
• Open an .asy file with Cmd+O, or
  • right-click a part and choose Edit its symbol (for a symbol from the schematic's folder), or
  • choose File → New Symbol, or New symbol in the canvas menu, to start an empty one.

docs.title: Draw it
docs.text:
• Lines: press W and click from point to point. A line can go at any angle. It ends when it reaches the end of another line or a pin; press Esc to end it anywhere.
  • Pins: press N, give the pin a name, and click where it goes. In the pin's dialog, Name shown sets where the name appears on a placed part, or hides it.
  • Text: press T for a comment.
  • Move, copy and delete lines, pins and texts like parts. The cross marks the symbol's origin: where a placed part sits on the grid.

docs.title: Set its attributes
docs.text:
Right-click the canvas and choose Symbol attributes….

  • Type: part (a component) or block (stands for the schematic of its name beside it; see Your own block).
  • Attributes: Prefix (R, C, X …), Value, Description, SpiceModel, ModelFile and others. A placed part takes them as its defaults.

docs.title: Save it
docs.text: Cmd+S saves the symbol. A new symbol's first save asks where; put it beside the schematics that place it. Its name is how schematics refer to it: one word, and not the name of a built-in symbol. Every open window with a schematic in the same folder draws the saved symbol anew.

docs.title: Keep a version history
docs.text: If a schematic lies in a git repository, nomospice shows its state and keeps a history of it. You need git installed.

docs.title: See the state
docs.text: The status bar shows the branch and whether the file is modified or not yet tracked. A schematic outside a repository shows no git; click it to open the History panel, where Initialize repository makes its folder a repository.

docs.title: Commit
docs.text: Open the History panel: View → Version History, or click the git state in the status bar. Save the schematic, type a message and click Commit. The list shows the commits of this file, the newest first.

docs.title: Compare and restore
docs.text:
Click Compare beside a commit: the canvas shows what has been added and removed since then, highlighted. Close comparison ends it.

Restore replaces the schematic with that version. It is an ordinary edit: Cmd+Z takes it back, and nothing is written until you save.

docs.title: Work with several windows
docs.text: Each window holds one schematic or symbol. Open as many as you like.

docs.title: Open windows
docs.text:
• Cmd+N (File → New Window) opens an empty window.
  • Cmd+O opens a file in the current window if it holds nothing yet, else in a new window.
  • A file is open in one window only: opening it again brings its window to the front. Opening it again from its own window reads it from disk again, after asking about unsaved changes.

On macOS, Window → Merge All Windows turns the windows into tabs of one window. The Window menu lists them all.

docs.title: Copy parts between schematics
docs.text: Select parts, press Cmd+C (or Cmd+X), go to the other window and press Cmd+V. The parts follow the mouse until you click to place them. Built-in and library symbols are found there too; a symbol from the first schematic's own folder must be in the other's folder as well. The same works between two running copies of nomospice, and the Edit menu's Cut, Copy and Paste do the same as the keys.

docs.title: Close and quit
docs.text:
• Cmd+W closes the window, after asking about unsaved changes. The last window is not closed but emptied.
  • Cmd+Q asks each window with unsaved changes in turn, bringing it to the front. Cancel in any of them keeps all windows open.

docs.title: Simulate in several windows
docs.text: Every window simulates on its own, and its Halt stops only its own run. All windows share one ngspice, which holds the results of the latest run only. If another window ran in between, nomospice runs again when you add a trace or export results. See One ngspice, many windows.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Keys and menus: every shortcut and menu item.
  • Analyses and directives: what nomospice runs, the forms that write it, numbers and expressions.
  • The plot window: mouse, table and menus of the plot.
  • Parts and symbols: the built-in symbols and default models.
  • Files and folders: file types, where settings and recovery copies live.
  • Command line and MCP: starting nomospice with a file, and its MCP tools.

docs.title: Analyses and directives
docs.text: nomospice runs ngspice. Directives are SPICE dot commands written as text in the schematic (press S). Most of them can be written with forms that show the line they write; typing SPICE directly works everywhere.

docs.title: Analyses
docs.text:
Written with the simulation command form (the toolbar's sliders). One analysis per kind runs; others are kept as commented alternatives in result tabs.

Directive Form tab Notes .tran Transient stop time, time step, start of saving, maximum step, uic .ac AC decade, octave or linear sweep; one frequency gives a phasor table .dc DC sweep a source, a parameter or temp; nested sweeps make curve families .noise Noise output and input source; spectra and totals .op DC op pnt the operating point as a table .tf Transfer fn gain, input and output resistance .pz Poles/zeros poles and zeros as a map in the s-plane .sens Sensitivity the sensitivities of an output to every part

docs.title: Other directives
docs.text:
Written with the directive form (S), its tabs in brackets.

Directive Does .param (Parameters) names a value: .param R=1k; use it in values as {R} or {R*2} .model (Model) a device model, its parameters explained in the form .meas (Measurement) a number measured after the run: a statistic over an interval, a value at a point, where a signal reaches a value, or the delay between two crossings .ic (Initial conditions) node voltages a transient starts from .temp (Temperature) the circuit temperature .include, .lib (Include file) a model file, whole or one section .step (Text) runs the analysis once per value: .step param C list 47n 100n 220n; also lin, oct, dec, a source's value, temp; up to three nested

Other dot commands that ngspice knows pass through as they are written.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
SPICE reads a number with a suffix, case-insensitively:

Suffix f p n u, µ m k Meg G T Factor 10⁻¹⁵ 10⁻¹² 10⁻⁹ 10⁻⁶ 10⁻³ 10³ 10⁶ 10⁹ 10¹²

1M is one milli, and 10F is ten femto. Value fields show how SPICE reads what you type and warn about these two.

docs.title: Values and expressions
docs.text:
• {expression}: a value computed from parameters, such as {R*2}.
  • mc(x, tol): x with a tolerance, uniform within ±tol (as a fraction); flat(x): uniform within ±x; gauss(x): normal with σ = x. They draw anew in each run of a .step, so .step param run 1 100 1 is a Monte Carlo analysis.
  • Laplace=H(s) on an e or g source: a transfer function, any ratio of polynomials in s.
  • Independent sources (V, I) are edited in a form: DC, sine, pulse, exponential, FM, piecewise linear (with a preview), an AC amplitude, and series resistance and parallel capacitance.

docs.title: Trace expressions
docs.text: Add trace takes ngspice expressions: V(out), V(a,b), I(R1), Ib(Q1) (a pin's current), arithmetic on them, and functions such as db(), ph(), group_delay(). Units follow from the expression: a voltage times a current is in watts, an integral of power in joules.

docs.title: Starting nomospice
docs.text:
nomospice [file] [--run]
nomospice --mcp
Argument Does file opens an .asc, .asy or netlist file at start --run runs the file's analysis once it is open --mcp starts the MCP server on standard input and output instead of the app

On macOS the program is nomospice.app/Contents/MacOS/nomospice.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Variable Does NGSPICE_LIB the ngspice shared library to load, instead of the one next to the program or the system's

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
The MCP server offers these tools to an AI assistant (see Let an AI assistant use nomospice). Each takes a schematic as path (an .asc or a netlist; absolute, or relative to where nomospice was started) or as asc text.

Tool Arguments Returns simulate path or asc; traces: ngspice expressions; points: samples per trace (default 200, at most 5000) the analysis and its scale, all vector names, operating-point values, .meas results, warnings, the log, and the traces asked for netlist path or asc the netlist with warnings, each item's nets, each part's current expression and pin names read_schematic path or asc parts (instance, symbol, value, pin nets), net labels, directives write_schematic path, asc, overwrite writes the file; an existing one only with overwrite library_search query, kind (a model type or SUBCKT), limit matching models and subcircuits library_get name the .model/.subckt text with its dependencies examples the example schematics as .asc text

docs.title: File types
docs.text:
Extension What nomospice .asc schematic opens and saves; Latin-1, or UTF-16 if needed; unknown lines kept .asy symbol opens and saves in the symbol editor; a block symbol's .asy lies beside its .asc .cir, .net, .sp, .spi, .ckt SPICE netlist opens as a schematic of one directive; saves as .asc beside it .lib, .sub, .mod, .inc … models included with .include/.lib; searchable when in a model library folder .svg picture exported schematic or plot .raw results exported, ngspice's binary format

Saving writes a new file next to the old one and then replaces it, so a failed save never leaves half a file.

docs.title: Where nomospice keeps its things
docs.text:
What Where model library list libraries.json in the configuration folder: ~/Library/Application Support/de.nomospice.app (macOS), %APPDATA%\de.nomospice.app (Windows), ~/.config/de.nomospice.app (Linux) recovery copies of unsaved work recovery-…json in the data folder: the same folder on macOS and Windows, ~/.local/share/de.nomospice.app on Linux a downloaded Micro-Cap 12 library libraries/Micro-Cap 12 in the data folder crash reports of the app itself panic.log in the configuration folder

The theme and the panel sizes are kept by the app's web view.

docs.title: Keys and menus
docs.text: The keys are the macOS ones. On Windows and Linux press Ctrl for Cmd. In nomospice, ? or F1 shows a short version of this page.

docs.title: Drawing
docs.text: Keys Does R C L D V I place a resistor, capacitor, inductor, diode, voltage or current source P, F2, Cmd+K any part: the component library (symbols, models, subcircuits) G ground W, F3 wire: click, click; Esc ends it N, F4 net label S SPICE directive (.tran, .param, .step …) T comment Cmd+R, Cmd+E (or Ctrl+R, Ctrl+E) rotate, mirror (the part being placed, or the selection) drag move parts; their wires follow M, F7 move parts off their wires; Esc or F8 ends it Cmd+C Cmd+X Cmd+V copy, cut, paste (also between windows) Cmd+D, F6 duplicate Cmd+Z, Shift+Cmd+Z undo, redo Cmd+A select all Del, Backspace delete the selection F5 the delete tool: click what goes Cmd+F find parts, labels, texts Space fit the view Cmd+=, Cmd+- zoom in, out double-click edit a part (value, model, its L/W/area) right-click a part's or the canvas' menu

docs.title: Simulating
docs.text: Keys Does Cmd+Enter run Cmd+L the log and the netlist

docs.title: Files and windows
docs.text: Keys Does Cmd+N new window Cmd+O open (here while this window is empty, else in a window of its own) Cmd+S, Shift+Cmd+S save, save as Cmd+W close the window (the last one is emptied) Cmd+, model libraries Cmd+Q quit (asks each window with unsaved changes)

docs.title: Plot
docs.text: Mouse Does click a wire, a part plot its voltage, its current (near a pin: that pin's current) click, shift-click cursor A, cursor B shift-drag the range A–B (average, RMS, integral) drag, wheel, double-click zoom; zoom and pan; see everything right-click a trace's row right axis, another unit's pane, group delay, remove right-click the plot FFT, Nyquist, Nichols, y axis, CSV, SVG, .raw

docs.title: The menu bar
docs.text:
Menu Items nomospice (macOS) About nomospice · Check for Updates… · Model Libraries… · Services · Hide · Quit File New Window · New Symbol · Open… · Close · Save · Save As… · Create Block Symbol… · Export Schematic as SVG… · Export Plot as SVG… · Export Results as .raw… · (Windows, Linux: Model Libraries…, Exit) Edit Undo · Redo · Cut · Copy · Paste · Duplicate · Delete · Select All · Rotate · Mirror · Find… Place Wire · Ground · Net Label… · Resistor · Capacitor · Inductor · Diode · Voltage Source · Current Source · Component… · Comment… · SPICE Directive… · Select · Move · Delete Mode Simulate Run · Halt · Edit Simulation Command… · Live Mode · Add Trace… View Fit to Window · Zoom In · Zoom Out · Log & Netlist · Version History · Light or Dark Theme · Back to the Schematic Above · Enter Full Screen (macOS) Window (macOS) Minimize · Zoom · the open windows · Merge All Windows Help Quick Reference · (Windows, Linux: Check for Updates…, About nomospice)

On Windows and Linux the menus show the keys but leave them to the window, so a key never runs twice.

docs.title: Built-in symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Part Prefix res resistor R cap, polcap capacitor, polarized capacitor C ind inductor L diode, zener, schottky, led diodes D npn, pnp bipolar transistors Q nmos, pmos MOSFETs M njf, pjf JFETs J voltage, current independent sources V, I e, g voltage-controlled voltage and current sources E, G sw, csw voltage- and current-controlled switches S, W opamp an op-amp (a subcircuit) X jumper a connection between two nets

The ground is a net label named 0.

docs.title: Default models
docs.text: Without a model library, these models are known: the diode 1N4148, the transistors 2N3904 and 2N3906, and switch models. More come from model libraries.

docs.title: Symbols from elsewhere
docs.text: A schematic's symbols are looked up in this order: the built-in symbols, the schematic's own folder, an installed LTspice's symbols, and the model library folders. A subcircuit without a symbol gets a generated box with its pins. A symbol of type block beside a schematic of the same name stands for that schematic: see Hierarchy.

docs.title: The plot window
docs.text: After a run with results over time, frequency or a sweep, the plot opens above the schematic. Drag the bar between them to share the space differently.

docs.title: Panes and axes
docs.text:
• Each unit has a pane of its own; the panes share the x axis and zoom together.
  • A trace can go on the pane's right axis, with a scale of its own, or into another unit's pane (on its right axis there).
  • AC results have two panes, magnitude in dB and phase in degrees, over a logarithmic frequency axis.
  • A .step makes every trace a family of curves, one per step; the table lists the steps.

docs.title: The table beside the plot
docs.text:
• one row per trace, with its value at the mouse, at cursor A and at cursor B;
  • with both cursors: Δx, 1/Δx and each trace's Δ; and the average, RMS and integral of each trace between them (without cursors: over the whole run);
  • .meas results under Measurements;
  • Add trace for an expression.

docs.title: Mouse
docs.text: Action Does click, shift-click sets cursor A, cursor B shift-drag marks the range A–B drag zooms into the range dragged over wheel or trackpad zooms around the mouse; sideways pans double-click shows everything again right-click a row right axis, another pane, group delay (AC), copy expression, remove right-click the plot its menu

docs.title: The plot's menu
docs.text: Reset zoom · Clear cursors · Add trace… · Bode, Nyquist and Nichols plot (AC) · FFT (spectrum) and back (transient) · Log y axis · Y range… · Copy data as CSV · Export plot as SVG… · Export results as .raw… · Remove all traces.

docs.title: Other result views
docs.text:
• A single-frequency AC analysis (.ac lin 1 50 50) gives a table of phasors, magnitude ∠ phase, under Phasors in the bottom panel.
  • .op, .tf and the totals of .noise are tables under Results or Operating point.
  • .pz shows the s-plane: see Find poles and zeros.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Four lessons that build on each other. Do them in order; each takes about ten minutes, and each ends with what you have learned.

  1. Your first simulation: draw an RC low-pass, run a transient analysis, probe a voltage and a current, measure with cursors.
  2. Frequency response: the same filter in an AC analysis: Bode plot, corner frequency, Nyquist plot, and two analyses in result tabs.
  3. Sweeps and measurements: run the filter for several capacitor values, measure each run, and simulate tolerances.
  4. Your own block: turn the filter into a block with its own symbol and use it twice.

You need nomospice installed. The tutorials use the macOS keys; on Windows and Linux press Ctrl where they say Cmd.

docs.title: Your own block
docs.text:
In this tutorial you turn the RC low-pass into a block: a part with its own symbol that stands for its schematic. You place it twice in another schematic to make a second-order filter, look inside it, and open its symbol in the symbol editor.

Start with the filter alone: the resistor, the capacitor to ground, and the labels in and out, without the source. Save it as rcfilter.asc in a folder of its own. The file name becomes the name of the block.

docs.title: Mark the ports
docs.text:
The labels are how the block connects to the outside. Double-click the label in and set its Port to input. Set the port of out to output in the same way. Ports are drawn as hexagons. Save the schematic.

Right-click an empty spot of the canvas and choose Create block symbol. nomospice writes rcfilter.asy beside the schematic: a box with the inputs on the left and the outputs on the right.

docs.title: Use the block
docs.text:
Make a new schematic with Cmd+N and save it in the same folder: a block is found beside the schematic that uses it. Press P for the component library. Search for rcfilter: it is listed as a block of rcfilter.asc, with its pins in and out. Place it like any other part.

Here two blocks are placed in series and driven by an AC source. Each block runs as a subcircuit of its schematic. The output falls off twice as steeply as one filter alone, 40 decibels per decade, and the label mid shows how the second filter loads the first.

Parameters

A block can take parameters: give the block the Value R=10k and use {R} in its schematic. A .param R=1k in the block's schematic is the default.

docs.title: Look inside
docs.text:
Right-click a block. Its menu can open the block's schematic and edit its symbol.

Open its schematic: nomospice shows rcfilter.asc in place of the schematic above, and the status bar shows the way back up. Click it to return.

Edit its symbol: the symbol opens on the canvas. Draw lines with the wire tool, add pins with the label tool, move and delete them like parts, and set the symbol's attributes from the canvas menu. Saved, the symbol is redrawn in every schematic of its folder.

docs.title: What you have done
docs.text:
• marked labels as ports and made a block symbol from a schematic;
  • placed the block twice and simulated the hierarchy;
  • opened a block's schematic and its symbol.

That is the end of the tutorials. The how-to guides show how to do particular tasks, and the reference lists every key, menu and directive.

docs.title: Your first simulation
docs.text:
In this tutorial you draw an RC low-pass filter, feed it a sine wave and look at what comes out: the two voltages, a current, and the delay between input and output. It takes about ten minutes.

When nomospice starts, it shows an empty schematic and a list of examples. You will start from scratch.

docs.title: Place the parts
docs.text:
Press V to pick up a voltage source. It follows the mouse. Click to put it down.

Press R for a resistor, and Ctrl+R to turn it on its side before you click. Then press C for a capacitor. Press Esc when you are done placing, and the space bar to fit the view. nomospice names the parts V1, R1 and C1 and gives each a default value.

docs.title: Wire them up
docs.text:
Press W for the wire tool. Click the top of the source, click again where the wire turns the corner, and click the left end of the resistor. The wire ends there because it reached a pin. Draw the second wire from the right end of the resistor to the top of the capacitor.

A circuit needs a ground. Press G and click under the source and under the capacitor. Then press N to name a net: enter the name in, click OK, and click the wire at the top of the source.

Name the other net out in the same way. Named nets are easier to find in the results, and the first run plots them for you.

docs.title: Set the values
docs.text:
Double-click the capacitor and type 100n. Next to the field, nomospice shows how SPICE reads it: 100 nanofarads.

1M is not a megohm

SPICE ignores case, so 1M means one milli. Write 1Meg for a million. The dialog warns you and offers the fix.

Double-click the source and choose Sine: an amplitude of 1 volt at 1 kilohertz. The preview shows the waveform, and the line below it shows the SPICE text the form writes.

docs.title: Run the simulation
docs.text:
Click the sliders in the toolbar to edit the simulation command. Choose Transient and a stop time of 3m, three milliseconds. Click OK, then click into the schematic to place the directive.

Press Cmd+Enter to run. The plot opens above the schematic with the voltages of the two named nets: the input sine, and the output, smaller and a little later.

docs.title: Probe and measure
docs.text:
Click the capacitor. Its current is added to the plot, in a pane of its own because it is a current, not a voltage. Clicking a wire plots its voltage the same way.

Click the plot to set cursor A, and shift-click to set cursor B. The table beside the plot shows each trace at both cursors and the difference between them. Here the output peaks 89 microseconds after the input: a phase of 32 degrees, just as the arctangent of 2πfRC predicts.

docs.title: What you have done
docs.text:
• placed parts with single keys, turned one with Ctrl+R, and wired them;
  • named nets and set values in forms that show the SPICE text they write;
  • run a transient analysis, probed a current by clicking a part, and measured with cursors.

Press Cmd+S to save the schematic as an .asc file. On Windows and Linux, use Ctrl wherever this guide says Cmd.

Next: Frequency response looks at the same filter in the frequency domain.

docs.title: Frequency response
docs.text:
In this tutorial you look at the RC low-pass of the first tutorial in the frequency domain: its Bode plot, its corner frequency, and its Nyquist plot. You keep the transient analysis as well, each in a result tab of its own.

Open the filter you saved, or the example rc_transient from the start screen. An AC analysis needs a source that drives it: double-click the source and enter an AC amplitude of 1. The sine stays for the transient analysis; the AC amplitude counts only in AC and noise analyses.

Press Cmd+Enter to run the transient analysis once more. Its result tab, Transient, sits above the plot.

docs.title: Add an AC analysis
docs.text:
Click the plus beside the Transient tab to add an analysis.

Choose AC. The form suggests a sweep of 100 points per decade from 10 hertz to 1 megahertz, which suits this filter. Click OK. nomospice writes the new analysis under the transient one as a comment, so the schematic's own analysis stays as it is, and gives it a result tab of its own, which opens and runs at once.

docs.title: Read the Bode plot
docs.text:
The AC tab's plot has two panes over a logarithmic frequency axis: the magnitude in decibels and the phase in degrees. The input is a flat line at 0 decibels and is left out; the output falls off above about a kilohertz.

Click the plot at about 1.59 kilohertz to set cursor A. The table shows −3 decibels and −45 degrees there: the corner frequency, 1 over 2π R C.

docs.title: Other views
docs.text:
Right-click the plot for its menu. Besides zoom, cursors and exports it offers two other views of an AC result: the Nyquist plot and the Nichols plot.

The Nyquist plot draws the imaginary part over the real part. A first-order low-pass is a half circle from 1 at low frequencies to 0 at high ones; cursor A is at its lowest point, the corner frequency. The cross at −1 is the point that matters for the stability of loops.

Click the Transient tab: its traces, zoom and cursors are as you left them. Each tab keeps its own results.

docs.title: What you have done
docs.text:
• given a source an AC amplitude for small-signal analyses;
  • added a second analysis as a result tab, and switched between the two;
  • read a corner frequency from the Bode plot, and seen the same result as a Nyquist plot.

Next: Sweeps and measurements runs the filter for several capacitor values and measures each.

docs.title: Sweeps and measurements
docs.text:
In this tutorial you run the RC low-pass for three capacitor values at once and let nomospice measure the corner frequency of each. At the end you see the same idea used for tolerances: a Monte Carlo analysis.

Open the example rc_bode from the start screen and run it. It is the filter of the previous tutorials with an AC analysis.

docs.title: Make the value a parameter
docs.text: Right-click the capacitor and choose Edit. Instead of a number, give it the value C in curly braces. The braces tell SPICE that this is an expression, here a parameter named C.

docs.title: Sweep it
docs.text:
Press S for a SPICE directive, and type a step command: dot step, param C, list 47n 100n 220n. Click OK and place it under the other directives.

Run it. The analysis now runs once for each value, and every trace becomes a family of curves. The table beside the plot lists the steps.

docs.title: Measure
docs.text:
Press S again and choose the Measurement tab. Name the result fc, and measure where a signal reaches a value: the output in decibels, vdb of out, reaching −3. The line below shows the dot meas command the form writes. Click OK and place it.

Run once more. The measurements appear beside the plot, one per step: 3.38 kilohertz for 47 nanofarads, 1.59 kilohertz for 100, and 722 hertz for 220, as 1 over 2π R C predicts.

docs.title: Tolerances: Monte Carlo
docs.text: The same mechanism handles tolerances. Open the example monte_carlo: its resistor is mc of 1k and 0.05, a value drawn anew within 5 percent in every run, and its capacitor varies by 20 percent. A step over a dummy parameter, run 1 to 20, repeats the analysis twenty times, and the measurement gives the spread of the corner frequency.

docs.title: What you have done
docs.text:
• used a parameter in curly braces as a part's value;
  • swept it with a step directive into a family of curves;
  • measured a quantity per step with a meas directive, written by a form;
  • seen tolerances simulated as a Monte Carlo analysis.

Next: Your own block turns the filter into a part you can place in other schematics.
